source.title: Improving Relative Representations with Learned Anchors and Whitened Inner Products
source.authors: Oscar Thorsted Svendsen; Nikolaj Holst Jakobsen; F. Mager; Hiba Nassar

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether representations from independently trained, heterogeneous encoders can be stitched with little loss, using relative representations but changing the anchor construction and similarity measure from the standard random-anchor/cosine setup.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates a deliberately constructed relative interface for zero-shot transfer; it does not measure whether unmodified representations naturally converge as model scale or capability increases. Rows cover the small-language-model retrieval results in Table 7, the aggregate alignment metrics in Table 4, and explicit ablation/support-set findings. Cited findings from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Tests V4 through held-out-encoder retrieval, classification and reconstruction using relative representations, and V6 through anchor, similarity and support-set ablations. Learning a mapping is part of V4; these experiments do not establish spontaneous convergence or convergence with scale.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct: the authors conclude that learned PARAM anchors and WIP improve alignment and zero-shot transfer across the tested vision, language and anisotropic reconstruction settings. Their stronger description of nearly lossless, universal communication should remain attributed to them: first-neighbour retrieval involving Gemma is incomplete, classification retains some losses, and exact affine invariance applies only without the shrinkage used in experiments.
record.recipe_differences: Retains the relative-representation and zero-shot-stitching framework, but replaces static random anchors with learned convex mixtures and cosine similarity with WIP; it also evaluates PARAM single-space and multi-space training.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with anchor construction and similarity (Random-WIP often underperforms Random-Cosine; WIP improves retrieval, especially with learned anchors), with single-space versus multi-space training, and with support-set size.
record.problems: The small-language-model test uses 3300 template-generated English sentences. The results evaluate a deliberately trained relative mapping, not spontaneous similarity of absolute representations. Several ablation and support-set results are given only in figures without extractable numerical values. The paper notes that stitching is not guaranteed under severe nonlinear distortions.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1 and 2 contain many pairwise image/text classification F1 results; omitted to stay within the 60-row limit, since the retained retrieval and geometry metrics more directly measure alignment. Table 3 repeats part of Table 7 and was omitted in favor of the fuller Table 7. Detailed MNIST figure values are unavailable in the text; only the stated qualitative result is recorded.

untested.parts: No relationship between model capability or scale and naturally learned representation alignment is measured.
No paired image-caption vision-language alignment experiment or capability trend.
The seeded autoencoders are evaluated through a constructed interface under induced anisotropy, not for naturally shared features or subspaces.
Unpaired alignment, layer stitching, unrestricted nonlinear mismatches and preservation of information beyond the tested tasks are not established.
No recurring interpretable neurons, SAE features or circuits are identified; learned semantic prototypes do not establish such recurrence.
No out-of-distribution evaluation, neighbour-setting sweep or empirical sweep of whitening shrinkage parameters. The tested dependence concerns constructed relative representations.
No natural-convergence plateau or causal comparison of shared training data, objectives and a common model of reality. Support-size saturation is a different phenomenon.

missing.what: Table 6 adds German, Spanish and Chinese evaluation encoders beyond Table 2; these results are neither recorded nor explicitly declared omitted. Include absolute references and matched cross-encoder F1 values, especially the PARAM Single residual losses: German/French classifier 82.64 ± 0.46 versus German absolute 89.20 ± 0.16. Table 6 also contains PARAM Multi results needed to distinguish training configurations.
missing.versions: V4; V6 for comparisons between interface configurations

record.verdict_notes: All Table 7 numerical values and encoder directions match the supplied text. V6 is supported by comparisons between rows; a row marked partial for V4 can contribute to an observed method-dependence result. Table 4 measures coordinate agreement, not downstream information loss, so its improvements alone do not warrant a nearly lossless-transfer verdict. Tables 1 and 2 are explicitly declared omitted and are not listed as missing. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Whether naturally learned representations of independently trained models become more aligned as model size or capability increases.
Alignment of vision and language representations on paired images and captions, and whether it rises with both models' performance.
Whether same-architecture models trained from different initializations learn shared features or subspaces; the autoencoder seed experiment evaluates stitching, not shared features.
Does not test stitching without paired data, layer stitching, or other mapping approaches beyond its relative-representation pipeline.
Whether interpretable features or circuits recur across models.
Tests selected anchor and similarity choices and support-set size, not a broad sweep of similarity metrics, neighbour settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.

Does not test whether natural convergence plateaus or whether shared training data/objectives explain convergence instead of a common model of reality. Its alignment objective is purposefully trained for the relative-space method.
